tldr: By unifying experiences across different humanoid robots and separating human-centered shared motion semantics from lightweight embodiment-specific modules, this work achieves joint multi-robot training and versatile whole-body control.
hero_caption: Overall concept of X-WBC. In simulation, nine different humanoids jointly train a single shared policy, learning shared human motion semantics. Below, four real humanoid robots with significantly different sizes and joint configurations are teleoperated using the same sparse VR input interface.
overview:
In recent years, humanoid Whole-Body Control (WBC) using large-scale human motion data has advanced rapidly. However, conventional methods typically train an individual policy from scratch for each robot. This leaves motion experience isolated across embodiments, preventing skills acquired on one robot from benefiting another.

This study focuses on a key insight: "the intent of human motion (semantics and temporal structure such as walking, kicking, or squatting) is embodiment-agnostic, but the joint movements that physically realize it vary across embodiments." The authors therefore propose "X-WBC," a framework that decouples shared motion semantics from embodiment-specific physical execution. Sparse VR signals (5 tracking points on the head and extremities), full human motion, and embodiment-specific reference motion are projected and aligned into a shared token space. A temporal Transformer backbone then learns from mixed rollouts across all robots.

In simulation experiments with nine humanoid embodiments, joint training achieved higher tracking performance than training on individual embodiments alone and showed strong robustness on an unseen motion dataset (100STYLE). Furthermore, across four real humanoid robots of varying sizes—Unitree G1, R1, H1-2, and H2—the authors succeeded in shared VR teleoperation using the same single control backbone.
contributions: Formulated a cross-embodiment joint training framework for humanoid whole-body control that shares experience across heterogeneous robots, replacing the traditional paradigm of training each robot in isolation.
Proposed a hierarchical policy architecture separating a shared human motion token space, a shared temporal Transformer backbone, and lightweight embodiment-specific input/output modules.
Demonstrated the effectiveness of joint training and realized whole-body control via a shared interface across nine simulated embodiments, an unseen external motion dataset, and four real robots.

sections.heading: Can robots bridge embodiment differences the way humans learn by watching others?
sections.summary: Humans can acquire skills by watching others despite differences in limb lengths and strength. This paper asks whether humanoid whole-body control can similarly learn shared motion representations across embodiments and share experience among multiple robots.
sections.details:
Even with different heights, limb lengths, and muscle strengths, humans can understand another person's intent by watching their movements and learn motor skills like kicking or squatting. In current humanoid whole-body control (WBC), however, it has been standard practice to retarget large-scale motion datasets to each robot's kinematics and train a separate policy per robot. As a result, valuable motion data and training experience remain isolated within each embodiment.

Meanwhile, in robotic manipulation, "robot foundation models" that train large-scale models on mixed datasets from diverse robots are achieving great success. The authors considered whether this approach could be brought into whole-body control.

The core insight here is that "the semantics of human motion data (geometric intent and temporal structure like walking or kicking) are embodiment-agnostic, but the joint motions that execute them are embodiment-specific." If shared motion semantics and robot-specific execution systems can be separated, rollouts from diverse robots can be used to optimize a single shared backbone. This led to the creation of "X-WBC," a cross-embodiment whole-body control framework evaluated across nine humanoid embodiments.

sections.heading: At the intersection of whole-body control, cross-embodiment foundation models, and human motion representations
sections.summary: This work connects single-embodiment humanoid whole-body control with insights from manipulation-focused cross-embodiment foundation models. It also positions human motion retargeting techniques as a projection route into a shared token space.
sections.details:
This study is situated at the intersection of three primary research areas:

### Humanoid Whole-Body Control (WBC)
Recently, works such as H2O, OmniH2O, HumanPlus, BeyondMimic, and SONIC have made motion tracking via imitation learning and reinforcement learning a standard interface for teleoperation and autonomous skill acquisition. However, all of these were trained specifically for a single robot morphology, with no attempts to share models across multiple embodiments.

### Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation Models
Studies such as RT-2, OpenVLA, $\pi_0$, and GR00T learn shared representations from heterogeneous robot datasets like Open X-Embodiment. They absorb embodiment differences using embodiment-conditioned adapters and related techniques, but they primarily target arm manipulation and vision-language-action models. This work extends that concept to closed-loop humanoid whole-body control, where maintaining balance and full-body dynamics is indispensable.

### Human Motion Representations for Humanoid Control
Retargeting techniques (such as GMR) that map human motion datasets like AMASS into robot joint spaces have continued to advance. In X-WBC, rather than treating these embodiment-specific reference motions as isolated supervision, they are utilized as one route to align full human motion and sparse VR signals into a shared latent space.

sections.heading: Decoupling shared semantics from embodiment-specific physics: X-WBC design and training
sections.summary: Motion inputs are projected into a shared token space, processed through a shared causal Transformer for temporal features, and converted into joint commands by embodiment-specific modules. Data from all embodiments is mixed into a single PPO batch for joint training.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Formulation of Cross-Embodiment Whole-Body Motion Tracking
Each robot $i$ is formulated as a Markov Decision Process $\mathcal{M}_i = (\mathcal{S}_i, \mathcal{A}_i, \mathcal{T}_i, \mathcal{R}, \gamma)$. While the state space $\mathcal{S}_i$, action space $\mathcal{A}_i$, and transition dynamics $\mathcal{T}_i$ are embodiment-specific, the reward function family $\mathcal{R}$ and discount factor $\gamma$ are shared across all embodiments.
The actor's observation consists of embodiment proprioception (joint positions/velocities, base angular velocity, gravity vector, and previous actions) and motion commands. The critic is also provided with privileged information such as link positions and base linear velocity. Because input and output dimensions vary across robots, zero-padding to the maximum dimension allows them to be mixed into a single mini-batch.

### 3.2 Human-Centered Command Encoding
Three input routes for motion commands are provided and projected into a shared token space:
- **Human motion encoder**: Takes full-body human motion from Mocap or similar sources as input, serving as an embodiment-agnostic motion anchor.
- **Robot motion encoder**: Takes dense reference motions retargeted to each embodiment as input, functioning as an embodiment-specific module.
- **Sparse VR encoder**: Takes only 5 keypoints (head and the extremities of hands and feet) as input. This interface enables low-latency teleoperation on real hardware without expensive Mocap setups.
During training, the mean squared error ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}$) among these three tokens generated from the same source motion is minimized to align the representations.

### 3.3 Shared Policy Backbone and Embodiment-Specific Modules
To capture motion phase and velocity trends, a causal Transformer backbone takes the past $L=32$ steps of observation token history as input. By leveraging a KV cache during online inference, it processes historical context while maintaining real-time performance (50Hz operation). The resulting action tokens are converted into target joint positions for each robot by lightweight embodiment-specific decoders, and torques are output by low-level PD controllers.

### 3.4 Joint Training Pipeline
Multiple robot simulation environments are built in parallel using Isaac Lab, and PPO jointly updates the shared backbone and embodiment-specific modules simultaneously. During rollouts, the three command token types are selected randomly with equal probability (1:1:1). Furthermore, training efficiency and Sim-to-Real robustness are enhanced by "adaptive motion sampling," which increases the sampling probability of motion segments that frequently cause falls or failures, along with domain randomization that perturbs contact parameters and center-of-mass positions.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of X-WBC. Three routes—sparse VR, full human motion, and embodiment reference motion—are aligned into a shared token space and fed into a shared causal Transformer backbone common to all embodiments. Final joint control is handled by lightweight proprioception encoders and action decoders selected by embodiment ID.

sections.heading: Versatility and tracking performance validated across 9 simulated embodiments and 4 real robots
sections.summary: Joint training surpassed single-embodiment training in tracking success rate and showed comparable generalization to existing single-embodiment models on unseen data (100STYLE). VR teleoperation was also demonstrated on four real humanoid robots of varying sizes.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Simulations used a total of nine humanoid embodiments: Unitree G1 (and its variants), H1, H1-2, R1, and H2, along with Fourier GR3, Booster T1, and Adam Lite. The BONES-SEED dataset (approximately 200 hours at 50Hz) was used for training, running for about two days on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

### 4.2 Architecture and Joint Training Benefits
In evaluations using BONES-SEED motions, X-WBC achieved a success rate (SR) of 98.60% on the Unitree G1, surpassing an MLP backbone baseline (97.70%) and a single-embodiment trained policy (97.69%). On the larger and more challenging H2, X-WBC reached 93.22% compared to 92.22% for single-embodiment training, clearly demonstrating the benefit of training with mixed experiences across multiple embodiments. In addition, tracking success rates remained comparable across different input formats (VR, robot motion, and full human motion), confirming successful token space alignment.

### 4.3 Generalization to Unseen External Motions (100STYLE)
Zero-shot generalization was evaluated with policy weights frozen on the independent "100STYLE" dataset (800 clips), which was not used in training. In comparisons on Unitree G1, X-WBC (sparse VR input) achieved a success rate of 91.13% (729 completed clips). This demonstrated high survival ability close to SONIC (93.00%), an existing state-of-the-art method specialized for a single embodiment, while significantly outperforming TWIST (75.62%).

### 4.4 Token Space Semantics and Real-World Deployment
In token space similarity retrieval experiments, Recall@1 reached 94.2% when retrieving the same motion across different input sources, and 76.1% across different robots. This demonstrates that shared motion semantics are preserved while embodiment-specific physical information is properly encoded.
For real-world evaluation, the policy was deployed on four physical robots: Unitree G1, R1, H1-2, and H2. The operator wore the same VR equipment (5 tracking points: head plus hand and foot controllers) and reliably controlled upper-body pose tracking, soccer ball kicking, and walking/running on grass across all robots despite differences in body size and joint counts.

captions.F4: Real-world deployment across four physical humanoid robots (G1, R1, H1-2, and H2). (a) shows upper-body pose tracking by the same VR operator, and (b) shows stable soccer kicking motions and outdoor running on grass.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Toward whole-body control foundation models that accumulate experience across robots
sections.summary: X-WBC shifts humanoid whole-body control from embodiment-isolated learning to cross-embodiment representation learning. Decoupling a shared backbone from embodiment-specific modules shows that sharing data across heterogeneous robots is a promising path toward WBC foundation models.
sections.details:
This research reframes humanoid whole-body control from "learning isolated controllers for each embodiment" to "learning shared representations across physical differences."

By aligning diverse input sources in a human-centered command token space, sharing temporal motion structure with a causal Transformer backbone, and delegating physical execution to lightweight embodiment-specific modules, its effectiveness was demonstrated across nine simulated embodiments and four physical robots. The fact that joint training achieved higher performance than individual embodiment training shows that aggregating and accumulating data from heterogeneous humanoids into a single foundation model is fully practical in the whole-body control domain.

sections.heading: Appendix: Shared reward design and training stabilization techniques
sections.summary: Details of the shared tracking and regularization reward functions across all robots, termination criteria, PPO hyperparameters, and adaptive motion sampling specifications to prevent overfitting and physical inconsistencies.
sections.details:
### Reward Design and Episode Termination Conditions
To provide fair learning signals across all robots, the reward functions adopt a shared formulation. In addition to tracking terms for base orientation, link position/orientation, and base velocity, penalty terms are imposed on sharp torque changes, joint limit violations, and unintended contacts other than the feet. Episode termination (fall detection) is strictly determined based on pelvis height error (0.25m or more), gravity vector misalignment, and end-effector vertical position errors.

### Adaptive Motion Sampling Details
To learn challenging motions efficiently, a mechanism dynamically increases the sampling probability of time bins (segments) where early terminations occur frequently. However, to avoid wasting training resources on retargeting failures or physically impossible motions, segments with persistently low success rates despite repeated attempts are completely removed from the working pool (hard removal) as a safeguard.

### Network Configurations and Domain Randomization
The Transformer backbone is maintained independently for the actor and critic, with an input token dimension of 256. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, ground friction coefficients, default joint angles, and base center-of-mass offsets are randomized, along with periodic velocity disturbances applied to the base.

takeaways: Decoupling "motion semantics (human-centered)" from "physical joint actuation (embodiment-specific)" allows joint training across multiple humanoids to improve control performance.

Aligning full-body Mocap, robot reference trajectories, and sparse VR signals (5 points) in a latent space enables dense supervision during training and flexible, lightweight VR control during real-world deployment.
Without specializing to a single embodiment, using appropriate shared representations and a causal Transformer maintains strong generalization survival rates on unseen motions (100STYLE).
limitations: Evaluation is primarily focused on Unitree-centric bipedal humanoids; how well it extends to morphologies with dramatically different limb proportions or joint arrangements remains unverified.
Embodiment-specific input/output adapters and individual retargeting procedures are still required, falling short of zero-shot morphology-conditioned adaptation to entirely unseen robots.

Real-world evaluations were limited to short-duration tasks such as upper-body poses, basic walking, and kicking; evaluation on complex rough terrain and long-horizon contact-rich tasks remains lacking.
